title: The Multi-Entity Reconciliation Guide for Businesses Operating Across Southeast Asia
summary: Multi-entity reconciliation in Southeast Asia slows the monthly close. Learn the four causes and the five capabilities your finance team should look for. The post The Multi-Entity Reconciliation Guide for Businesses Operating Across Southeast Asia appeared first on Xendit .
body_markdown:
**Multi-entity reconciliation** in Southeast Asia has become one of the


**heaviest recurring workloads** a regional finance team carries, and the transaction volume behind it keeps climbing.


Reconciliation is the accounting process of comparing two sets of financial records, your internal ledger against what your payment provider, bank, or another entity reports, so discrepancies surface and get resolved early


.


For a business running


**several legal entities** ,


**currencies** , and


**payment channels** across the region, that comparison determines how quickly you can close your books each month, how much of your finance team's capacity goes to matching records instead of analysis, and


how confidently you can report how much each entity holds and what the group position is.


In 2025,


[digital payments gross transaction value (GTV) across ASEAN-10](https://www.temasek.com.sg/content/dam/temasek-corporate/news-and-views/resources/reports/e-conomy-sea-2025-report.pdf) reached around USD 1.41 trillion, up from USD 1.17 trillion in 2024, with a projection of approximately


**USD 2.4 trillion** to


**USD 2.6 trillion** by


**2030** .


Each additional transaction is another line your team has to match against a settlement record and book under the correct entity.


Finance teams are responding by automating more of that work.


In


[Deloitte's SEA CFO Agenda 2025](https://www.deloitte.com/content/dam/assets-zone1/southeast-asia/en/docs/services/consulting/2025/sea-cxo-cfo-agenda-2025.pdf) ,


**59% of CFOs** said they expect to


**embed more automation** or digital technologies into their operations. Within the finance function specifically, respondents named accounting, reporting, and reconciliations among the most promising areas for AI at 48%.


Reconciliation is now one of the finance processes companies plan to automate.


**Here’s what this article covers:**


- Why multi-entity reconciliation gets harder as your business adds entities, currencies, and payment channels


- What fragmented and manual reconciliation costs your finance team at month-end close


- The five capabilities that separate reconciliation infrastructure built to scale from one that adds work with every entity


- How Xendit supports entity-level separation, transaction-level reporting, and multi-currency records


- What your business can take from a regional company that shortened its monthly close while transaction volume grew


## **Why multi-entity reconciliation becomes harder as your business grows**


As your business expands across markets, reconciliation gets harder because financial data no longer comes from one system, one currency, or one operating process.


There are


**four conditions** that make multi-entity reconciliation harder as your business adds more entities, currencies, and payment channels:


### **1. Fragmented systems and reporting formats**


Different entities may use separate payment providers, accounting systems, and internal tools, each producing transaction data in its own format. Your team consolidates those records before reconciliation can begin, and the work grows for regional businesses where reports have to be collected market by market or entity by entity.


The practical effect on your business is that the close date depends on the slowest entity to report. Reconciliation teams also receive different formats across payment methods,


so your team has to reformat every file into one template before it can start comparing records.


### **2. Separately managed processes across entities**


Subsidiaries and business units often follow their own reconciliation, settlement, and reporting workflows. When those processes are managed independently, with separate owners and separate improvement goals, finance teams end up with inconsistent records and extra coordination work at consolidation.


The cost lands on your business twice. Central finance spends time aligning records that were never designed to line up, and two teams can invest in overlapping tools without knowing it, so the group pays for capability it could have bought once.


### **3. Multi-currency transactions add more values to reconcile**


Operating across Southeast Asia can mean a customer pays in one currency while funds are converted and settled in another. Your team then connects the original transaction amount, the converted value, the FX (foreign exchange) rate applied, the settlement currency, and the final net amount,


so


all five values can be traced back to the same payment.


When any of those values are missing from the report, the gap between what the customer paid and what reached your account becomes something your team reconstructs manually.


Each difference your team cannot explain, for example a payment that lands smaller than the amount charged, holds up the close and becomes something your auditors will ask you to support with a record.


### **4. Manual processes increase reconciliation workload**


When transaction data cannot be consolidated automatically, your team spends more hours collecting reports, matching records, validating discrepancies, and preparing data for closing.


[Manual work also raises error risk](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20210316005058/en/Duco-Manual-Process-Errors-Top-List-of-Data-Reconciliation-Pain-Points-for-Financial-Firms-During-Pandemic) as volumes climb, and 28% of financial services organizations identify mistakes from manual processes as their single biggest data reconciliation pain point, ahead of a lack of operational data at 19% and operational risk at 15%.


For a growing business, this puts a ceiling on expansion.


A manual process that still works at your current transaction volume becomes the constraint on how many entities and markets you can add before the close stops fitting inside your reporting calendar.


None of these four conditions stay inside the reconciliation task. The delays and errors they create show up in your reporting deadlines, your team's capacity, and how clearly your leadership can see the financial position of the business.


## **The cost of fragmented reconciliation when closing your monthly books**


Fragmented systems, separate workflows, multi-currency records, and manual matching each add


**delay** and


**error** to the closing process.


**Four costs** appear consistently, and each one gets bigger as transaction volume increases:


**1. Longer monthly financial close and delayed reporting**


Your management team receives the monthly financial results later than planned, which delays the decisions that depend on them, such as adjusting budgets or approving spending in a new market.


**2. Higher operational workload for finance teams**


Collecting, formatting, and matching records takes a large share of your finance team's time, which is the capacity your business could spend on forecasting, margin analysis, and market planning.


**3. Greater risk of errors and unresolved discrepancies**


Manual entry and manual matching produce mistakes, such as a transaction recorded under the wrong entity or a fee counted twice, and each one takes time to find and correct. Unresolved differences carry through to the audit.


**4. Limited visibility into entity-level and group-wide financial positions**


Without a reliable view of both entity-level and group-wide positions, your business cannot quickly say how much any single entity holds and what the group position looks like today.


These costs grow fastest in the businesses that are expanding fastest, since every new entity, market, and payment channel adds records to a process that is still manual.


The pattern behind all four costs is the same. Your finance team ends up repairing records after the fact, when the detail needed to match them could have been attached to each transaction from the start. That moves the question away from how your team reconciles and onto what your payment and reporting systems hand them to work with.


## **What regional finance teams need from scalable reconciliation infrastructure**


Reducing the amount of reconciliation your team has to do manually depends on what your payment and reporting layer can produce without manual assembly.


There are


**five capabilities** that separate reconciliation infrastructure built to scale from a setup that adds work with every new entity:


### **1. Entity-level separation with group-wide visibility**


Your team needs each entity or business unit to have its own balance and transaction history, while still being able to view regional activity centrally.


Both views serve different purposes, since entity-level records support statutory reporting and internal accountability, while the group view supports treasury decisions and consolidated reporting.


### **2. A consistent transaction trail**


Every transaction should retain enough information to connect payment, fee, settlement, and any refund, payout, or other balance movement that follows it. When that relationship is preserved in the record, your team verifies it in one pass. When it is missing, your team rebuilds it manually from separate reports.


### **3. Settlement-aware reporting**


Finance teams need to distinguish transactions that have occurred from money movements that have actually settled. This matters most around month-end, when the transaction date and the settlement date can fall into different reporting periods and a payment recorded in one month reaches the balance in the following month.


### **4. Clear multi-currency records**


When a payment involves a currency conversion, reporting should preserve the original transaction currency alongside the converted and settlement values. With those figures on the same record, your team can point to the rate and fees that explain the difference. Without them, FX becomes a black box your finance and audit teams have to open manually.


### **5. Data that can flow into existing finance processes**


At regional scale, reconciliation should not depend on downloading files and manipulating spreadsheets. Reports need to be exportable, scheduled, or accessible by API so they connect to the ERP, accounting, or internal finance systems your team already runs, which keeps


the numbers in your reconciliation record and your general ledger the same.


Getting all five in place across several markets depends on where the records come from, since they have to be connected at the point the transaction is created. That makes the


**payment provider** handling your transactions as important to your close as the accounting system receiving the numbers.

Your team reconciles by matching on the reference or transaction ID, confirming the transacting amount against the order record, and confirming the net amount against the credit on the balance. The whole


**currency path stays visible** , so an FX difference becomes something your team can explain in a note.


**Mekari** , an Indonesian business software company serving thousands of merchants, previously needed a five-person team and around 10 days each month to


**reconcile millions of transactions manually** between its internal dashboard and its payment gateway dashboard. Because transaction data could not be separated across thousands of merchants,


**the** **books were often not balanced** despite the effort, and


**the team could not know each merchant's balance** with certainty.


[Mekari implemented Xendit's Platform Payments](https://www.xendit.co/en/case-study/mekari/) to create a


[sub-account](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/sub-accounts) for each of its merchants, with


**transactions recorded automatically** under


**separate ledgers** showing the starting and finishing balance for each one. The balance and transaction tabs then served as the reference point for the whole business, and


**clean per-merchant reporting** , including admin fees, could be downloaded from the dashboard without manual calculation.


The


**results** changed how the finance function operates:


- **Reconciliation manpower fell by 60%** , down to a team of two


- The


**monthly reconciliation cycle shortened** to 2 to 3 days


- **Reconciliation ran 5x faster** overall


- **Merchant balances became accurately available** **from a centralized source** , so the team could confirm what each merchant was able to withdraw


Mekari's


**payment volume grew 140%** from 2021 to 2022, so the


**reconciliation workload came down** while transaction volume climbed.


The takeaway for your business is the shape of that curve.


**Scalable reconciliation lets transaction volume and entity count grow** without finance headcount and month-end workload growing at the same rate.

## **FAQ for regional finance teams in Southeast Asia: Multi-entity reconciliation**


### **How do you reconcile transactions across multiple business entities in Southeast Asia?**


Start by keeping each entity's balance and transaction history separate at the payment layer, so records do not have to be untangled later at consolidation. With


**Xendit** , your business can create


[sub-accounts](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/sub-accounts) for branches, subsidiaries, merchants, or business units under one master account through


[XenPlatform](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/xenplatform-overview) , each with an isolated balance and its own ledger. Your team reconciles at the entity level and views activity across accounts centrally from the same dashboard.


### **Can you keep separate balances for each subsidiary and still see the total across the group?**


Yes, and both views are needed for different purposes, with entity-level records for statutory reporting and internal accountability, and a group view for treasury and consolidated reporting.


**Xendit's**[Accounts Overview](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/xenplatform-monitoring-transactions#accounts-overview) shows every


[sub-account](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/sub-accounts) with its status and current cash balance, while each account keeps its own


[transaction](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/transactions-report) and


[balance](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/balance-report) history. Your head office gets the consolidated picture without losing the separation your entity reporting depends on.


### **How do you reconcile a payment when the customer pays in one currency and you settle in another?**


You need the full currency path on the same record, covering the transacting amount, the converted amount, the settlement currency, the net amount, and the FX rate applied.


**Xendit's**[transaction reporting](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/transactions-report) exposes each of these as its own column for


[multi-currency card payments](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/card-multi-currency-processing) , so your team can match on the reference or transaction ID and tie the original charge to the credit on your balance. That removes the manual reconstruction FX differences usually require.


### **Why does the monthly financial close take so long for businesses operating across multiple countries?**


Most of the delay comes from assembling data before matching can start, since entities may run on different providers and systems, formats differ by payment method, and settlement dates can fall outside the transaction month.


**Xendit** produces


[transaction-level](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/transactions-report) and


[balance-level reports](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/balance-report) in one consistent structure across accounts, including


[settlement](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/balance-report) status and settlement date on each transaction line.


Your team then spends the closing period checking the few transactions that do not match, instead of rebuilding reports.


### **Can reconciliation reports be delivered automatically instead of downloaded manually?**


Yes. The


[Xendit Transactions Report](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/transactions-report) and


[Balance Report](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/balance-report) can be exported on demand from the dashboard, scheduled for automatic delivery to email or an SFTP server, or generated through the report API. That lets your finance data reach your ERP or accounting system on a set schedule.


### **Do you need a separate payment provider for each entity you operate in Southeast Asia?**


No, and running a different provider per entity is one of the main reasons reporting formats diverge and consolidation turns manual. With


**Xendit** , your business can onboard multiple entities as


[sub-accounts](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/sub-accounts) under


[one platform account](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/xenplatform-overview) and keep transaction routing, fee handling, and reporting consistent across them. Adding an entity becomes a configuration step instead of a new integration with a new reconciliation process attached to it.
